source_text: Deinde quis parasitus ita militis gloriosi vires assentationibus extulit, ut Traducianus diaboli? Quod de ponderibus affectuum agnosci licet. Fecit siquidem Deus hominem, materiam ipsam limi venerabili dignatione contrectans, quae in formam hominis auctoris sui manum subacta sequeretur. Steterat iam absolutum, ceterum pallens frigensque simulacrum, spiritum quo niteret et vigeret opperiens. Tunc augustissimo auctoris afflatu creatus et inspiratus animus, viscera impleta commovit; tunc omnes sensus in apparatum propriorum munerum suscitati sunt. Dedit habitator ingressus visceribus colorem, sanguini calorem, membris vigorem, cuti nitorem. Vide quod negotium in formando et animando homine pietas divina suscepit. Verum nec perfectum eum reliquit familiaritas Conditoris; transfertur ad amoeniorem locum, et quem clementer fecerat, munifice locupletat. Nec hoc tamen praestitisse contentus, illustrat eum impertitione colloquii; dat ei praeceptum, ut libertatem suam intellegens, videret sibi suppetere per quod fieret amicior Conditori; quod praeceptum non in multa distenditur, ne quid oneris de multiplicata lege sentiret; sed interdictu unius pomuli, testimonium devotionis expetitur. Postea quoque ut haberet consortem, per quam pater fieret, denuo illius manus, qua conditus erat, nobilitatur attactu; divino quoque subinde colloquio fovetur atque honoratur. Haec ergo a Deo praestita tam longa, tam multa, tam grandia, instituta, munera, praecepta, colloquia, nullam fecerunt homini boni necessitatem; at e regione diabolus non minus timide, quam callide, exigua cum muliere verba commiscuit; et tantum virium habuisse dicuntur, ut continuo in conditionem naturalium verterentur; immo ingenita cuncta subruerent, facerent perpetuam mali necessitatem, et dominum ac possessorem imagini Dei diabolum imponerent. Quid ergo fortius, quid excellentius, quid magnificentius adversaria potestate, si tantum levi confabulatione fecit, quantum Deus nec operibus suis potuit, nec muneribus obtinere? Manifestum est itaque, in eius vos parte consistere, cuius tam immodice potentiam praedicatis; nec in cultum Dei nostri ullum habere consortium, quem nos ut aequissimum, ita omnipotentissimum confitemur, qui potens est, et veritas in circuitu eius, qui humiliat sicut vulneratum superbum, id est, diabolum et Manichaeum, vosque eius asseclas calumniantes naturam, ne vos sponte peccare fateamini. Ipse ergo Deus noster in virtute brachii sui disperdit inimicos suos [n110] , per quod nihil aut a vobis, aut a Manichaeis afferri potuit, quod non veritatis eius fulmine dissiliret.
pass_a_gloss: Then who as a parasite so lifted the powers of a glorious soldier by flatteries, as the Traducian those of the devil? Which it is allowed to be recognized from the weights of affections. For God made the human, handling the matter itself of mud by a venerable condescension, which subjected would follow the hand of its author into the form of a human. Already an absolute, but pale and cold image had stood, waiting a spirit by which it would shine and thrive. Then by the most august breath of the author a mind created and inspired moved the filled viscera; then all the senses were stirred into an apparatus of their own gifts. The inhabitant having entered gave color to the viscera, heat to the blood, vigor to the members, polish to the skin. See what business divine piety took up in forming and animating the human. But the familiarity of the Founder did not leave him even unfinished; he is transferred to a more pleasant place, and him whom he had made clemently he richly enriches. Nor nevertheless content to have furnished this, he illustrates him by an imparting of conversation; he gives him a precept, that understanding his freedom he would see that there was available for him that through which he would become more a friend to the Founder; which precept is not stretched into many things, lest he feel something of a burden from a multiplied law; but by the interdict of one little fruit a testimony of devotion is sought. Afterward also that he might have a partner through whom he would become a father, again that hand by which he had been founded is ennobled by a touch; he is also forthwith cherished and honored by a divine conversation. These things therefore furnished by God so long, so many, so great, institutions, gifts, precepts, conversations, made no necessity of good for the human; but from the opposite side the devil no less timidly than cunningly mixed slight words with the woman; and they are said to have had so much powers, that they were immediately turned into a condition of natural things; nay they undermined all inborn things, made a perpetual necessity of evil, and imposed the devil as lord and possessor on the image of God. What therefore stronger, what more excellent, what more magnificent than an adversary power, if by a light conversation it made so much, as God could obtain neither by his works nor by gifts? It is therefore manifest that you stand on his side, whose power you preach so immoderately; nor have any fellowship in the cult of our God, whom we confess as most equitable, so most omnipotent, who is powerful, and truth in his circuit, who humbles the proud as wounded, that is the devil and Manichaeus, and you his followers calumniating nature, lest you confess you sin spontaneously. Our God himself therefore in the virtue of his arm destroys his enemies, through which nothing could be brought either by you or by the Manichaeans which would not burst apart by the thunderbolt of his truth.

pass_b_english: What parasite ever flattered a boastful soldier’s strength as the advocate of inherited sin flatters the devil’s? This can be recognized by weighing their respective influences. God made the human being, handling the very material of clay with an awe-inspiring condescension, as it followed its author’s hand into human shape. The completed image stood there, still pale and cold, awaiting the breath through which it would shine and live. Then the soul, created and breathed in by the author’s most august breath, stirred the inward parts it filled. Every sense awakened to prepare for its own tasks. The entering inhabitant gave color to the inward parts, warmth to the blood, vigor to the limbs, brightness to the skin. See the work divine goodness undertook in forming and animating humanity (Genesis 2:7)!

Yet the Creator’s closeness did not abandon him once complete. He was transferred to a more delightful place; the one God had mercifully made he generously enriched. Nor, content with this, did God stop there: he enlightened him by sharing conversation. He gave him a command so that, understanding his freedom, he might see the means at hand to become closer to his Creator. The command was not stretched into many provisions, lest a multiplied law impose a burden. The prohibition of one small fruit sought evidence of devotion. Later, so that he might have a companion through whom to become a father, he was ennobled again by the touch of the hand that made him. Divine conversation continued to cherish and honor him (Genesis 2:8–25).

These divine provisions—so prolonged, so many, so great: arrangements, gifts, commands, conversations—created no necessity of good in humanity. On the other side, however, the devil, as timid as he was crafty, exchanged a few words with the woman. Those words are said to have had such power that they immediately became a natural condition—indeed, overthrew every inborn thing, created perpetual necessity of evil, and imposed the devil as lord and possessor over God’s image.

What, then, is stronger, more excellent, more magnificent than the hostile power, if with a slight conversation it accomplished what God could obtain neither by his works nor by his gifts? Plainly you stand on the side of the one whose power you proclaim so excessively. You have no share in worshiping our God, whom we acknowledge as both perfectly fair and all-powerful: ‘He is mighty, and truth surrounds him’; he humbles the proud one as a wounded man—that is, the devil and Mani, and you their followers, who slander nature to avoid admitting that you sin voluntarily. Our God, then, ‘scatters his enemies by the strength of his arm’ (Psalm 89:8, 10; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 88:9, 11). Thus neither you nor the Manichaeans could bring forward anything that the thunderbolt of his truth did not shatter.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
